content: Allergic conjunctivitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the conjunctiva, which is the thin membrane covering the white part of the eye. This inflammation is triggered by an allergic reaction. The primary symptoms include redness, which is mainly caused by the dilation of small peripheral blood vessels, swelling (edema) of the conjunctiva, itching, and excessive tearing. When allergic conjunctivitis occurs alongside rhinitis, the condition is referred to as allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Epidemiologically, allergic conjunctivitis demonstrates distinct patterns depending on the population studied and the presence of coexisting conditions. Females are more commonly affected, and children often present with other concurrent allergic diseases. The condition typically manifests in intermittent episodes, although chronic forms are more frequently encountered in clinical practice. The natural course of allergic conjunctivitis is generally non-progressive, with a favorable prognosis. Most symptoms resolve on their own, but certain subtypes may show an association with specific age groups and triggers. Rare but serious complications can occur, including infections, scarring, and damage to the cornea and eyelids. The long-term outlook is influenced by the recurrence of episodes and potential side effects of treatment. The diagnosis of allergic conjunctivitis often involves a detailed history, including a personal or family history of allergies or atopy, as well as previous similar episodes. The hallmark symptoms are itching and diffuse redness of the bulbar and tarsal conjunctiva, which are nearly universal across all subtypes. Additional symptoms may include eye pain, discharge, sensitivity to light (photophobia), and visual disturbances. On physical examination, conjunctival redness (hyperemia) and discharge are commonly observed. Specific clinical signs may include Horner-Tranta's dots, shield ulcers, and a cobblestone appearance in vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC); a sandpaper-like texture of the eyelids in atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC); and giant conjunctival papillae in giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC). Further diagnostic studies may involve conjunctival scrapings, which can reveal inflammatory infiltrates. Tear analysis may show elevated levels of inflammatory mediators such as histamine and prostaglandins. Treatment for allergic conjunctivitis focuses on targeting various points in the inflammatory cascade. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical for secondary prevention of the condition. Emerging therapies include the use of immunomodulators and the exploration of novel enzymatic targets to manage the disease more effectively.
